You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: low frequency, mid load; Ip = 25 uA peak, f = 50 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 680 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: high frequency, small Cp, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 200 Hz, Cp = 17.5 nF, RL = 4700 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: low frequency, large Cp; Ip = 25 uA peak, f = 50 Hz, Cp = 32.5 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: high frequency, large Cp, heavy load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 200 Hz, Cp = 32.5 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: hot, heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 200 kOhm, temperature 85 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a load $R_L$ from a storage capacitor $C_{out}$ (node "out").
    *   Constraints: $V_{out,min} \ge 1.8\text{ V}$, $V_{out,max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$, Ripple $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{ V}$, Startup $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{ s}$, Settled $dv \le 0.02\text{ V}$.
    *   Piezo: Sinusoidal current source $I_p \sin(2\pi ft)$ in parallel with $C_p$ and $20\text{ M}\Omega$.
    *   Open-circuit voltage $V_{oc} \approx 3.2\text{ V}$ (at S1).

    *   `SyncBridge_Zener` (Score 67.98):
        *   Passed 4/6. Failing: S2 ripple (60 mV), S6 ripple (64 mV).
        *   Connectivity: Synchronous switches instead of diodes for a full-bridge.
        *   $S_1, S_2, S_3, S_4$ switches. $G_1$ (pos peak) and $G_2$ (neg peak).
        *   Zener $D_1$ (0 to out) for overvoltage protection.
        *   Essentially a synchronous rectifier.
    *   `PSSHI_Zener` (Score 62.48):
        *   Passed 4/6. Failing: S2 settled, S4 settled, S2 ripple, S4 ripple.
        *   Connectivity: Partial SSHI (Parallel Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor). $L_1, S_1$ invert the piezo voltage. Full bridge $D_1-D_4$.
    *   `FBR_Zener` (Score 22.10):
        *   Passed 1/6. Failed on power (S4, S5, S6) and timing (S2).
    *   `Hybrid_SSHI_Sync`: Failed completely. Negative voltage.

    *   `SyncBridge_Zener` is very close. Only ripple on S2 (low freq, mid load) and S6 (hot, heavy load) is an issue.
    *   The issue "ripple is too large... the storage cannot buffer the charge pulses against the load" suggests we might need a slightly different way to deliver charge or more efficient extraction.
    *   However, if the budget for $C_{out}$ is limited (max 47 uF), the ripple $V_{pp} = \frac{I_{load} \cdot T}{C_{out}}$ might be the limiting factor. Wait, the components allow up to 47 uF. `SyncBridge_Zener` used $9.2\text{ e-7 F}$ (0.92 uF). This is very small. Increasing $C_{out}$ would reduce ripple.
    *   But the evolution strategy already tries to optimize values. If the optimizer can't find a $C$ that satisfies both $t_{up}$ and ripple, it's a tradeoff:
        *   Larger $C \rightarrow$ Lower ripple, but slower $t_{up}$ and possibly worse `settled` (longer time constant).
        *   Smaller $C \rightarrow$ Faster $t_{up}$, but higher ripple.

    *   Wait, `SyncBridge_Zener` has $t_{up}$ okay for all. The failing ripple is $60\text{ mV}$ vs $50\text{ mV}$. This is very close.
    *   If `SyncBridge_Zener` is almost there, how can we improve it?
    *   Maybe a SEH (Synchronous Electric Harvesting) or an SSHI (Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor) variant that extracts more energy, allowing the storage to stay fuller or enabling a larger $C$ while still meeting $t_{up}$.
    *   Standard SSHI uses an inductor to invert the piezo capacitance voltage at the peaks. This significantly increases the harvested energy.

    *   *Standard SSHI Topology:*
        1.  Piezo $C_p$ charges.
        2.  At peak, a switch closes $L$ across $C_p$ for $t_{on} \approx \pi\sqrt{L C_p}$ to flip the voltage.
        3.  The flipped voltage is then rectified to the storage capacitor.

    *   Let's try a "Synchronous-SSHI" (SSHI with synchronous rectification).
    *   Structure:
        *   $L_1$ and $S_{inv}$ for inversion.
        *   Full-bridge (can be switches or diodes) to transfer energy to $C_{out}$.

    *   Actually, look at the `SyncBridge_Zener` again. It's a synchronous full bridge.
    *   What if we add an inductor-based inversion stage (SSHI) *before* the synchronous bridge?
    *   Wait, the `PSSHI_Zener` already did a version of this (L-S in parallel with piezo, then FBR). It failed on `settled` for S2 and S4. This suggests the energy pulses are too sparse or the storage is too slow.

    *   Let's try a more robust SSHI:
        *   $L_1, S_1$ (invert)
        *   $S_2, S_3, S_4, S_5$ (sync bridge)
        *   Wait, that's too many switches. Limit is 4 switches.

    *   Let's try a "Synchronous-SSHI" using a simplified rectification:
        *   $S_{inv}$ (invert: pzp to pzn via $L_1$)
        *   $S_{rect1}$ (pzp to out)
        *   $S_{rect2}$ (pzn to out)
        *   $S_{rect3}$ (0 to pzn/pzp?) - no.

    *   Let's consider an active rectifier (synchronous) combined with an SSHI inversion.
        *   Switch 1: $S_{inv}$ (pzp $\rightarrow$ $L_1$ $\rightarrow$ pzn) for inversion.
        *   Switch 2: $S_{pos}$ (pzp $\rightarrow$ out)
        *   Switch 3: $S_{neg}$ (pzn $\rightarrow$ out)
        *   Switch 4: $S_{gnd}$ (0 $\rightarrow$ pzp/pzn) -- this is getting complex.

    *   Let's try a different approach: a "Charge Pump" or a "Boost" style? No, the piezo is a current source.

    *   Let's go back to `SyncBridge_Zener`. It's almost perfect. The only problem is ripple on S2 and S6.
        S2: low freq (50 Hz), mid load ($680\text{ k}\Omega$).
        S6: nominal freq (100 Hz), heavy load ($200\text{ k}\Omega$).
        The ripple is $V_{pp} \approx \frac{I_{load} \cdot T}{C_{out}}$.
        For S6: $I_{load} = 2.05\text{ V} / 200\text{ k}\Omega \approx 10.25\text{ $\mu$A}$. $T = 0.01\text{ s}$.
        $V_{pp} \approx (10.25\text{ $\mu$A} \cdot 0.01\text{ s}) / C_{out} = 1.025\text{e-7} / C_{out}$.
        If $V_{pp} = 0.064\text{ V}$, then $C_{out} \approx 1.6\text{ $\mu$F}$.
        To get $V_{pp} < 0.05\text{ V}$, we need $C_{out} > 2\text{ $\mu$F}$.
        But $t_{up}$ must be $\le 0.4\text{ s}$.
        $t_{up} \approx \frac{C_{out} \cdot V_{out}}{P_{avg}/V_{out}} = \frac{C_{out} \cdot V_{out}^2}{P_{avg}}$.
        If $C_{out}$ is too large, $t_{up}$ fails.

    *   Wait, if the power extracted $P_{avg}$ is higher, we can afford a larger $C_{out}$ while keeping $t_{up}$ constant.
        `SyncBridge_Zener` is basically a synchronous rectifier. It doesn't do voltage inversion (SSHI).
        SSHI can significantly increase $P_{avg}$ by reducing the charge that has to flow back and forth in the piezo capacitor.

    *   Let's propose an SSHI circuit with a synchronous rectifier.
        *   $L_1$ and $S_1$ for inversion.
        *   Since we only have 4 switches total, we can use 1 for inversion and 3 for rectification, or 1 for inversion and 2 for a half-bridge (with diodes).
        *   Wait, a simpler SSHI:
            *   $S_1$: $L_1$ from pzp to pzn (invert).
            *   $D_1, D_2, D_3, D_4$: Full bridge rectifier.
            *   $C_1$: Storage.
            *   $D_5$: Zener clamp.
            *   This is exactly `PSSHI_Zener`!
            *   `PSSHI_Zener` failed on `settled` for S2 and S4.
            *   S2: $f=50\text{ Hz}, R_L=680\text{ k}\Omega$.
            *   S4: $f=50\text{ Hz}, R_L=1000\text{ k}\Omega$.
            *   `settled` means $|mean(0.7-0.8) - mean(0.6-0.7)| \le 0.02\text{ V}$.
            *   The drift is due to the time constant $R_L C_{out}$ being too large.
            *   For S4: $R_L = 4.7\text{ M}\Omega$ (wait, S4 is $1\text{ M}\Omega$).
